questions.question: What is a stateless service?

options.text: A service that stores all data
A service that doesn't retain client state between requests

questions.explanation: Stateless service treats each request independently—no memory of previous requests. All needed information comes with the request. Any instance can handle any request. Easier to scale horizontally.

questions.question: What is a stateful service?

options.text: A service in a specific US state
A service that maintains client state between requests

questions.explanation: Stateful service remembers previous interactions—maintains session data, connection state, or cached context. Requests may depend on previous requests. Requires routing to same instance or shared state.

questions.question: Which are advantages of stateless services? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Simple load balancing—any instance can handle any request
Better fault tolerance—instance failure doesn't lose state

questions.explanation: Stateless advantages: easy scaling (add instances), simple load balancing (no sticky sessions), fault tolerance (restart instance, no state lost). Latency may actually be higher if state must be fetched each request.

questions.question: Which are advantages of stateful services? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Lower latency when state is needed—no external fetch
Simpler for certain use cases (WebSocket connections, gaming)

questions.explanation: Stateful advantages: lower latency (state in memory), natural fit for connections (WebSockets, gaming), efficient for state-heavy operations. NOT easier to scale—scaling stateful services is complex.

questions.question: How can stateful services be scaled?

options.text: Sticky sessions, state externalization, or partitioning by key

questions.explanation: Stateful scaling options: sticky sessions (route user to same instance), externalize state (Redis, database), partition by key (user X always goes to instance Y). Each has trade-offs in complexity and performance.

questions.question: A web application stores user sessions in memory on each server. What problem does this create?

options.text: Users lose session if routed to different server or server restarts

questions.explanation: In-memory sessions make the app stateful. If load balancer routes user to different server, session is lost. If server restarts, all sessions lost. Solutions: sticky sessions, external session store (Redis), or stateless tokens.

questions.question: What is session affinity (sticky sessions)?

options.text: Load balancer routing all requests from a user to the same server instance

questions.explanation: Sticky sessions: load balancer ensures user's requests go to same instance (using cookies, IP). Enables stateful services but creates uneven load distribution and problems when instances fail.

questions.question: True or False: REST APIs should be stateless.
questions.explanation: REST constraint: statelessness. Each request contains all information needed—server doesn't store client state between requests. Enables scalability, caching, and reliability. Authentication via tokens, not server-side sessions.

questions.question: Which services are typically stateful? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Stateful services: WebSocket servers (maintain connections), databases (store data), gaming servers (game state). REST APIs should be stateless by design—state in external stores or tokens.

questions.question: How does externalizing state help with scaling?

options.text: Services become stateless; state is in shared store accessible by any instance

questions.explanation: Externalizing state (to Redis, database): services become stateless, any instance can handle any request by fetching state from shared store. Enables horizontal scaling. Trade-off: added latency for state access.

questions.question: A chat application needs to maintain WebSocket connections. What's the best approach?

options.text: Accept stateful nature; use pub/sub for cross-instance messaging

questions.explanation: WebSocket connections are inherently stateful. Accept this; scale using pub/sub (Redis) to broadcast messages across instances. Each instance manages its connections; pub/sub coordinates cross-instance communication.

questions.question: What happens to in-flight requests when a stateful server instance crashes?

options.text: Requests fail; state is lost unless externalized or replicated

questions.explanation: Stateful instance crash: in-flight requests fail, in-memory state is lost. Users may need to re-authenticate, reconnect, or lose work. Mitigation: replicate state, checkpoint to external store, or design for recovery.
